name: Phentermine

lead: Phentermine is a prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite and has been used for short-term weight loss since 1959. It is the most prescribed obesity drug in the US, according to reviews.
Weight loss is modest, about 3.6 kg over placebo at 12 weeks per one summary, and smaller than with newer injectable drugs.

paras: It is an amphetamine-like sympathomimetic amine that releases norepinephrine in the brain, which reduces hunger.

Labels warn of rare pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease, and of effects like raised blood pressure, insomnia and dependence-related withdrawal. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and is a controlled substance. The fen-phen episode of the 1990s involved heart valve damage.

lead: Phentermine is a sympathomimetic amine with an amphetamine-like profile, sold by prescription as an appetite suppressant and approved in the US as a short-term adjunct, usually described as a few weeks, to diet, exercise and behavior change in adults with obesity [1][2]. Grokipedia dates its FDA approval to 1959 and lists brands including Adipex-P, Lomaira and Duromine [2].

Reviews report that it is the commonly prescribed and that it produces modest weight loss compared with newer incretin drugs; Grokipedia cites about 3.6 kg more than placebo over 12 weeks [3][4][2]. It is also one of the two components of phentermine/topiramate (Qsymia), which was studied in the CONQUER, SEQUEL and EQUIP trials [5][6][7].

Phentermine is also remembered for the fenfluramine-phentermine (fen-phen) combination, which was linked to valvular heart disease in a 1997 report, leading to the withdrawal of fenfluramine [8][9]. The US label lists rare pulmonary hypertension and valvular heart disease as warnings [1].
infobox: Prescription-only; Schedule IV in the US

paras: The label indicates phentermine as a short-term adjunct in weight reduction for patients with an initial BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with risk factors such as controlled hypertension, diabetes or hyperlipidemia [1]. Grokipedia states that longer off-label use has been studied and that prescribing to adolescents has risen [2].

Appearance interest is in fat loss and appetite control. Grokipedia describes the drug as a stimulant; the label notes that sympathomimetic anorectics are pharmacologically similar to amphetamine [2][1].

Network meta-analyses and reviews of obesity drugs include phentermine, usually combined with topiramate, among the available options and show smaller effects than semaglutide or tirzepatide [4][3][10][11]. The CONQUER phase 3 trial tested two doses of low-dose controlled-release phentermine plus topiramate against placebo [5]; SEQUEL followed participants for two years [6]; EQUIP studied severely obese adults [7]. A 2025 trial analyzed predictors of BMI reduction on phentermine/topiramate in adolescents [12], and a 2021 trial compared it with exenatide and dapagliflozin in polycystic ovary syndrome [13].

Registered studies include a 600-person trial of intermittent phentermine, a long-term effectiveness study of 870 participants, a trial in patients undergoing bariatric surgery and a pilot on eating behavior [14][15][16][17]. A pharmacokinetic study characterized steady-state levels of extended-release capsules [18].

The label describes rare primary pulmonary hypertension and serious regurgitant cardiac valvular disease, effects on hazardous tasks, and withdrawal effects after prolonged high dosing; it advises against combining it with other weight-loss drugs [1]. Phentermine is contraindicated in pregnancy [1]. Grokipedia reports contraindication in cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism and uncontrolled hypertension [2]. The 1997 fenfluramine-phentermine report documented valve disease and later work linked fenfluramine's valve effects to 5-HT2B receptors [8][9].

Phentermine promotes norepinephrine release; amphetamine-type stimulants release norepinephrine more potently than dopamine or serotonin [19][2]. The label states it has not been established that appetite suppression is the primary action [1].
Phentermine is a prescription-only controlled substance in the US [2]. The combination with fenfluramine in the 1990s became a public-health case study [8].
